items.title: Clicks vs clients
items.script: Most people judge an ad by clicks. Clicks are cheap and they prove nothing. The number that matters is cost per booked consultation. Track the whole path, from the first click to the signed client, or you are guessing with real money.

items.title: What a Meta Pixel is
items.script: A Meta Pixel is a small piece of code on your website. It tells Meta what a visitor did, like viewing a page or booking a call. Meta uses that to find more people like them. No pixel, no learning, and the algorithm is flying blind.

items.title: The first three seconds
items.script: On social, people decide almost instantly whether to keep watching. Your opening has to earn the next few seconds. Lead with the problem or the surprising result, not your logo. Put the context after you have their attention.

items.title: Search intent versus scroll intent
items.script: Someone searching for a lawyer or a med spa has a problem right now. Someone scrolling Instagram is just killing time. Same business, different mindset. Search catches people ready to act. Social builds trust before they are ready. Use each for what it does best.

items.title: AI and missed calls
items.script: If your office phone goes to voicemail, many callers just call the next business. An AI receptionist can answer instantly, ask the right questions, and book the appointment. It does not replace your team. It catches what your team cannot get to.

items.title: Why ads stop working
items.script: Ads get tired. When people see the same image again and again, they stop noticing it. Your numbers slip and you blame the platform. Often the fix is simple. Refresh the creative, test a new angle, and keep the offer clear.

items.title: One page, one action
items.script: You paid for the click. Now do not waste it. A landing page should ask for one thing, a call or a booking, and make it easy. Every extra link, menu, or option is another reason for the visitor to leave.

items.title: Where AI actually helps
items.script: AI is great at the boring work. Drafting first versions, sorting leads, answering common questions, summarizing calls. It is weak at judgment and trust. Use it to give your team more time for the human parts, not to replace them.

items.title: Brand versus performance
items.script: Performance marketing harvests demand that already exists. Brand marketing creates it. If you only run performance, you slowly run out of people who know you. A healthy plan funds both, and measures each one differently.

items.title: The funnel in plain English
items.script: Every customer moves through three stages. They notice you, they consider you, then they decide. Most wasted ad spend comes from showing a decision message to someone who has only just noticed you. Match the message to the stage.

items.title: Which post drove the sale (UTM tags)
items.caption:
Which post actually drove the sale? Most teams cannot answer that, and the fix takes about two minutes per link.

UTM tags are short labels added to the end of a link. When someone clicks, your analytics tool reads the label and tells you exactly where that visit came from.

Do this today:
1. Pick three tags for every link you share: source (instagram), medium (social or email or paid), and campaign (the name of the push, like fall_launch).
2. Use the same spelling and lowercase every time. "Instagram" and "instagram" show up as two different sources.
3. Keep a simple sheet with the naming rule so everyone on your team follows it.
4. Open your analytics tool after a week and compare campaigns side by side.

Swipe through for the full breakdown. Save this for your next link, and send it to whoever builds your links.

#utmtracking #marketinganalytics #digitalmarketing #adops

items.title: Ad metrics decoded
items.caption:
Four numbers show up in almost every ad report. Here is what each one means and what to check first.

CPM: what you pay to be shown 1,000 times.
CTR: out of everyone who saw the ad, how many clicked.
CPC: what you pay for one click.
CPA: what you pay for one result, like a lead or a sale.

Do this today:
1. Open your last report and find all four numbers for each campaign.
2. If CPM is high, attention is getting expensive. Look at the audience and the creative.
3. If CTR is low, the message is not matching the person. Test a new hook.
4. If CPA is high while clicks look fine, check the step after the click.
5. Change one thing at a time, then re-check in a week.

Save this for report day. Comment "metrics" if you want the next post to go deeper on one of them.

#adspend #paidmedia #marketingmetrics #digitalmarketing

items.title: Audience size
items.caption:
Is your ad audience too narrow or too broad? Both cost you, in different ways.

Too narrow: the platform has little room to learn, delivery stalls, and prices climb.
Too broad: the message tries to speak to everyone, and you get clicks from people who were never a fit.

Do this today:
1. Start with a clear location. Be specific about where your customers actually are.
2. Add one or two interests, or none at all, and let the platform find people.
3. Run it for a full week before judging.
4. If delivery stalls, widen a little. If clicks come from the wrong people, tighten the targeting or sharpen the message.

Swipe for the full checklist. Save this for your next campaign.

#metaads #facebookads #adtargeting #digitalmarketing

items.title: Retargeting explained
items.caption:
Retargeting means showing ads to people who already know you. That is why it needs a different message than a first hello.

Who to include:
1. Website visitors from the last few weeks
2. People who watched a good portion of your videos
3. People who engaged with your Instagram profile or posts

Do this today:
1. Build one retargeting audience, starting with website visitors.
2. Keep the window short so the audience stays warm. Fewer days usually means a fresher audience.
3. Write a message for someone who has already seen you: answer a common question, show a result, or make the next step easy.
4. Do not reuse your cold ad. Warm people need a different message.

Save this for your next campaign, and send it to whoever runs your ads.

#retargeting #remarketing #metaads #digitalmarketing

items.title: Lookalike audiences
items.caption:
A lookalike audience finds new people who resemble your best customers. The quality of the result depends almost entirely on the list you start with.

That starting list is called the seed.

Do this today:
1. Export a list of real buyers, not just visitors or followers.
2. Use recent customers, because they reflect who is buying now.
3. Make sure the list is large enough for the platform to use. Check the platform's minimum size.
4. Upload it as a custom audience, then create the lookalike from it.
5. Test it against a broad audience and compare results after a week.

Better seed, better lookalike. Swipe for the checklist and save this for your next audience.

#lookalikeaudience #metaads #adtargeting #digitalmarketing

items.title: Attribution windows
items.caption:
Why do two reports show different sales for the same campaign? Usually it comes down to the attribution window.

7-day click counts a sale if someone clicked your ad and bought within 7 days.
1-day view counts a sale if someone saw your ad, did not click, and bought within a day.

Same sale, different rules, different numbers.

Do this today:
1. Check which attribution window each report uses. It is usually in the column settings.
2. Match the window across reports before you compare them.
3. Match the date range, including the time zone.
4. Match the definition of a conversion, so you are counting the same event.
5. Write the window next to every number you share.

Save this for report day, and send it to anyone who compares dashboards.

#attribution #marketinganalytics #metaads #adops

items.title: Keyword match types
items.caption:
In Google Ads, match types decide which searches can trigger your ad. Choosing the right one controls both reach and waste.

Broad: the widest reach, related searches included, and the least control.
Phrase: searches that carry the meaning of your keyword.
Exact: searches with the same meaning as your keyword.

Do this today:
1. Start tighter, with phrase or exact on your best keywords.
2. Open the search terms report and read the real searches that triggered your ads.
3. Add the ones that fit as keywords, and block the ones that do not.
4. Widen only the keywords that have earned it.

Control first, reach second. Swipe for the full guide and save this for your next search campaign.

#googleads #searchads #ppc #paidmedia

items.title: Negative keywords
items.caption:
Negative keywords tell Google what NOT to show your ad for. They are one of the simplest ways to stop wasting budget on searches that were never going to convert.

Example: a law firm adds the words "free" and "jobs" so people looking for free help or employment do not click.

Do this today:
1. Open the search terms report in Google Ads.
2. Scan for searches that do not fit what you offer.
3. Add those words as negative keywords.
4. Repeat every week. The list gets sharper and your spend gets cleaner over time.

Swipe for the steps. Save this for your next review and share it with whoever manages your search ads.

#googleads #ppc #searchads #paidmedia

items.title: Google Quality Score
items.caption:
Google gives each keyword a Quality Score from 1 to 10. It looks at three things, and better quality can lower your cost per click.

1. Expected click rate
2. Ad relevance
3. Landing page experience

Do this today:
1. Group keywords by theme, so each ad group covers one idea.
2. Write ads that mirror the words people actually search.
3. Make sure the landing page delivers what the ad promised.
4. Check the Quality Score columns in your keyword view and start with the lowest scores.

Relevance is rewarded. Swipe for the breakdown and save this for your next search campaign.

#googleads #qualityscore #ppc #paidmedia

items.title: Reach vs impressions
items.caption:
Reach and impressions sound alike, but they answer different questions.

Reach: how many different people saw your ad.
Impressions: how many times your ad was shown.

Example: one person who sees your ad 3 times is 1 reach and 3 impressions.

Do this today:
1. Use reach when you want to know the size of the audience you touched.
2. Use impressions when you want to track volume.
3. Compare the two to see how often each person is seeing the ad.
4. Label which one you mean whenever you share a report.

Save this for report day, and send it to a teammate who mixes them up.

#adreporting #marketingmetrics #metaads #digitalmarketing

items.title: The learning phase
items.caption:
New ads often wobble in the first days. That is the learning phase, and it is normal.

During it, the platform is still testing who to show your ad to. Meta looks for about 50 results in 7 days per ad set to exit it, so results can swing from day to day until then.

Do this today:
1. Avoid editing budgets, audiences, or creative every day while it learns.
2. Make sure your budget is large enough to reach that number of results for your chosen goal.
3. Use fewer ad sets so each one gets enough data.
4. Judge performance after the learning period, not on day two.

Patience is a strategy. Swipe for the common mistakes and save this for your next launch.

#metaads #facebookads #adlearning #digitalmarketing

items.title: Campaign structure
items.caption:
Every ad account is organized in three levels, and knowing what lives at each one keeps your testing clean.

Campaign: the goal.
Ad set: the audience, budget, schedule, and placements.
Ad: the creative and the copy.

Do this today:
1. Choose the goal first, since everything else follows from it.
2. Define the audience in the ad set.
3. Build the creative last, and test one thing at a time.
4. Name each level clearly, so you can read your reports later.

Goal first, creative last. Swipe for the full guide and save this for your next build.

#metaads #adstructure #paidmedia #digitalmarketing

items.title: Incrementality
items.caption:
Did your ad cause the sale, or did it just get the credit? That is the difference between attribution and incrementality.

Attribution shows who saw an ad and then bought. Incrementality asks who would NOT have bought without the ad. Some buyers were already on their way.

Run a simple test:
1. Hold out a region or an audience, and do not show them the ads.
2. Run the ads for everyone else for a set period.
3. Compare results between the two groups.
4. The gap between them is your true lift.

Swipe for the steps. Save this for your next test, and send it to whoever reports your results.

#incrementality #marketingmeasurement #paidmedia #adops

items.title: Conversion lag
items.caption:
Do your most recent days always look weaker than the rest? That is probably conversion lag.

Conversion lag is the time between an ad click and the purchase. People click today and buy later, so the last few days of a report keep filling in.

Do this today:
1. Find your typical delay. Look at how long past customers took from first click to purchase.
2. Avoid judging yesterday or the day before.
3. Compare matured days only, meaning days where the full lag window has passed.
4. Expect longer lag for bigger decisions.

Give the numbers time to arrive before you make a call. Swipe for the steps and save this for report day.

#conversionlag #marketinganalytics #metaads #adops

items.title: Campaign naming
items.caption:
Messy campaign names make reports hard to read, hard to filter, and hard to hand off. The fix is one naming pattern that everyone uses.

A simple pattern:
1. Platform and objective, like meta_leads
2. Audience and creative, like warm_video3
3. Start date, like oct

Put together: meta_leads_warm_video3_oct

Do this today:
1. Agree on the pattern with your team.
2. Write it in a shared doc.
3. Use it for every campaign, ad set, and ad from now on.
4. Rename old ones when you next touch them.

Name it once, read it forever. Save this for your next build.

#campaignnaming #adops #marketingops #paidmedia

items.title: Daily vs lifetime budget
items.caption:
Daily budget or lifetime budget? Both work, but they suit different plans.

Daily budget: an average amount per day. Best for always-on campaigns. Spend can vary a little from day to day.
Lifetime budget: a total for the whole run. Best for campaigns with fixed start and end dates. The platform paces spend across the dates.

Do this today:
1. Ask whether the campaign has a fixed end date.
2. If it does, consider a lifetime budget with a clear schedule.
3. If it runs continuously, use a daily budget.
4. Check pacing after the first few days.

Match the budget to the plan. Swipe for the full guide and save this for your next launch.

#metaads #adbudget #paidmedia #digitalmarketing

items.title: Ad placements
items.caption:
Where does your ad actually show? In Meta Ads, placements decide whether people see it in feeds, stories, or reels.

Automatic placements: the platform spreads your ad across them.
Manual placements: you choose each one yourself.

Do this today:
1. Start with automatic placements.
2. After a week, open the placement breakdown in your report.
3. Remove the placements that clearly do not work for your goal.
4. Build creative that fits: vertical for stories and reels, square or portrait for feeds, and keep key text away from the edges.

One idea, several formats. Swipe for the checklist and save this for your next campaign.

#metaads #adplacements #paidsocial #digitalmarketing

items.title: Bid strategies
items.caption:
A bid strategy tells the platform how to spend your budget. Here are three common choices in Meta Ads.

Lowest cost: spend the budget to get the most results.
Cost cap: aim for an average cost per result.
Bid cap: set the most you will pay in any single auction.

A simple path:
1. Start with lowest cost so the platform can learn.
2. Learn your typical cost per result.
3. Then test a cost cap, using that number as your target.
4. Change one thing at a time.

Control comes after data. Swipe for the steps and save this for your next campaign.

#metaads #bidstrategy #paidmedia #digitalmarketing

items.title: Contrast and readability
items.caption:
Can people read your design in half a second? Contrast decides.

Text needs strong contrast against its background. If it is hard to read, it will not be read.

Do this today:
1. Squint at your design, or switch it to grayscale. If the text fades, the contrast is too weak.
2. Fix it with a darker overlay, a bigger size, or a heavier weight.
3. View it on a phone, since that is where most people will see it.
4. Step back from the screen. If you hesitate to read it, fix it.

Swipe for the checklist. Save this for your next design, and send it to your designer.

#graphicdesign #designtips #socialmediadesign #branding

items.title: Type hierarchy
items.caption:
Type hierarchy decides what the eye reads first. Three simple tools control it: size, weight, and space.

Size: bigger reads first.
Weight: bolder stands out.
Space: room around text gives it importance.

Do this today:
1. Decide the single most important line in your design.
2. Make it the biggest and boldest element.
3. Add one supporting line, smaller and lighter.
4. Keep small details for last, and stop at three levels. More levels add noise.

Swipe for the full guide and save this for your next layout.

#typography #graphicdesign #designtips #socialmediadesign

items.title: Brand style guide basics
items.caption:
A brand style guide does not need to be a 50-page document. One page is enough to start, and it keeps every post looking like the same brand.

Consistency builds memory. When posts look different, people take longer to recognize you.

Do this today:
1. List your colors with exact codes.
2. Pick two fonts and write where each one is used.
3. Add logo spacing and size rules.
4. Share the page with everyone who makes content, and add more rules as you grow.

Swipe for the starter page. Save this for your team.

#brandidentity #brandguidelines #graphicdesign #branding

items.title: The creative brief
items.caption:
A creative brief is five lines that can save a week of back and forth.

What goes in it:
1. The goal
2. The audience
3. The one message
4. The proof
5. The next step

Do this today:
1. Write the brief on one page before any design or video work starts.
2. Keep to one message. If there are three, there are none.
3. Add proof: a result, a quote, or a demo.
4. State what the viewer should do next.

A clear brief makes better creative every time. Swipe for the breakdown and save this for your next project.

#creativebrief #contentcreation #marketingtips #creativeprocess

items.title: Giving creative feedback
items.caption:
"I don't like it" gives a designer nothing to work with. Specific feedback beats loud feedback.

Use this format:
1. The goal we are aiming for
2. What is not working yet
3. One thing to try next

Do this today:
1. Before you comment, restate the goal in one sentence.
2. Name the problem, not the fix, when you are unsure of the solution.
3. Suggest one direction to try, and keep the rest for the next round.
4. Problem first, solution second.

Swipe for the format. Save this for your next review and send it to your team.

#creativefeedback #designprocess #creativedirection #marketingteam

items.title: A better AI prompt
items.caption:
Better input, better output. A good AI prompt has five parts.

1. Role: who it should act as
2. Task: what to do
3. Context: what it needs to know
4. Format: how to answer
5. Limits: what to avoid

Example. Vague: "Write a post about ads." Clear: "Act as a social editor. Write 3 caption options for a carousel on retargeting. Plain language. No hype."

Do this today:
1. Rewrite one of your usual prompts with all five parts.
2. Compare the result to what you got before.
3. Edit the draft like a human.

Swipe for the example and save this for your next prompt.

#aiprompts #aimarketing #promptengineering #contentcreation

items.title: Fact-check your AI
items.caption:
AI can state wrong things in a confident tone. Confident is not correct.

The risk is highest in names, numbers, dates, and sources.

Do this before anything goes live:
1. Check every number and name.
2. Open the source yourself and confirm it says what the draft claims.
3. Read the text aloud to check the tone.
4. Have a person sign off, every time.

AI drafts. People decide. Swipe for the checklist and save this for your team.

#aimarketing #aitools #contentcreation #marketingops

items.title: Build a prompt library
items.caption:
If everyone on your team rewrites the same prompts, results vary from person to person. A shared prompt library fixes that.

Do this today:
1. Save the prompts that worked.
2. Label each one by task, like "caption draft" or "ad headline options".
3. Add a sample output next to each one so others know what good looks like.
4. Review the library once a month and remove what no longer works.

A shared library keeps quality steady and saves time. Swipe for the steps and save this for your team.

#aiworkflow #promptengineering #aimarketing #marketingops
